A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UMA research work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching retained results across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training experiments, empirical scaling laws, architectural ablations, inference benchmarks, and evaluations across multiple chemical domains.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds UMA-S-1.2 results, cross-architecture MoLE experiments, and diatomic evaluations.

M1.justification: Appendix A.7 introduces UMA-S-1.2 with charge balancing in L0 channels, task-specific output heads, single-atom prediction support, 64 rather than 32 experts, and 32 rather than 64 radial basis functions. It also replaces direct-force pretraining followed by conservative fine-tuning with conservative training throughout. These substantially revise the model and training procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix A.7 and Table 10 expand training beyond the original datasets with OPoly26 polymers, OC22 oxide electrocatalysts, OC25 solid-liquid interfaces, and single-atom and diatomic data. Appendix G adds diatomic bond-separation evaluations. Full-OMol25 training for UMA-1/1.1 was already documented in v1 and is not new coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix F.2 adds an OMol25 comparison of MoLE-equipped and ordinary EquiformerV2 models alongside corresponding eSEN controls. EquiformerV2's earlier materials/catalysis comparisons did not cover this experiment. The eSEN-sm-cons baseline emphasized in v2's main tables already appeared in v1's appendix.

E3.justification: UMA-S-1.2 introduces FP32 and 300 maximum neighbors throughout training, a two-plus-one-epoch schedule, and revised sampling ratios separating OMat24 AIMD and rattled structures. Appendix F.2 introduces controls using 6M base parameters and eight training epochs. Table 2 changes molecular energy reporting from per-atom to total energy, while inference benchmarking adds a newer software/backend configuration without updating historical timings.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's expert-count and single-task/multitask analyses, v2 tests MoLE across eSEN and EquiformerV2 architectures and analyzes expert usage by dataset. Appendix G adds diatomic failure analysis comparing UMA-S-1.1 with UMA-S-1.2, plus a controlled comparison of UMA-S-1.2 trained with and without diatomic data.

E5.justification: Figure 6 newly reports dataset-wise variances of expert routing coefficients alongside their means, extending v1's mean-only expert visualization with descriptive variability. This does not establish repeated-training uncertainty. The scaling-law procedure using 1,000 bootstrap samples and 10th/90th percentile bounds remains unchanged.

E6.justification: v2 adds UMA-S-1.2 benchmark and timing results and new architectural and diatomic results. Table 26 reports OMol diatomic energy MAEs of 2429.5 and 60.5 meV without and with diatomic training data, respectively. Some existing results are also revised: UMA-M-1.1 Dist-LR is 214.8 meV in v1 Table 12 and 138.1 in v2 Table 4, although the old value remains in v2's appendix. Many other UMA-1.1 values merely move into the main tables.

T1.justification: The MoLE linear-combination identities, equivariance reasoning, energy referencing, and scaling-law derivations remain unchanged. The new model description and empirical analyses introduce no new formal definitions, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: universal cross-domain atomic models, empirical scaling laws, efficient MoLE capacity scaling, and performance competitive with specialized models. The new model and analyses do not redefine these main claims.

C2.justification: Appendix G substantially expands applicability qualifications by distinguishing smooth diatomic curves from accurate predictions and explaining residual dissociation failures through global charge/spin assignments and the cutoff envelope. It also tentatively attributes an N-N barrier to training data. Appendix F adds interpretations of expert sharing and architectural generality, while Section 4.4 replaces the molecular chemical-accuracy assertion with a more qualified DFT-surrogate interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix A.7 and Tables 9–10 add extensive UMA-S-1.2 configuration, optimization, epoch, and sampling information. Appendix D specifies fairchem 2.16.0 requirements and the umas_fast_gpu execution backend for small systems. These materially expand reproducibility information, although A.7 explicitly defers further implementation details.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for OPoly26 and OC25 to support the expanded training data. The related-work discussion and positioning relative to universal MLIPs, mixture-of-experts approaches, and scaling-law research remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section structure are retained. Local changes include rewriting the molecular-results paragraph, adding version-specific notes and Appendix A.7, subdividing Appendix F, and appending Appendix G. This is a localized extension rather than extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds expert mean/variance heatmaps, three paired diatomic-curve figures, and new configuration, sampling, architectural-comparison, and diatomic-result tables. Main tables also change model selection, comparator grouping, metric headers, and timing columns. Original Figures 1–5 and historical appendix tables are retained, so their relocation and renumbering are not additions.

improvement.justification: The architectural controls and diatomic ablations strengthen validation beyond v1, particularly by separating smoothness from accuracy and documenting remaining physical failure modes. These gains are tempered by deferred UMA-S-1.2 details and inconsistent reporting: v2 Table 2 uses total-energy headers while retaining baseline numbers labeled per-atom in v1 Table 11, and updated molecular scores are not reconciled with retained appendix values. The net improvement is useful but limited.
